title: Decide authoring format (JSON vs Markdown+front-matter) — schema/tooling/runner depend on it
context: open-coding-curriculum is an open CC-BY (prose) / MIT (code) curriculum of beginner programming lessons with graded, runnable exercises across languages. Every exercise carries a reference solution proven correct in CI (solutionVerified:true), learner code runs zero-install in-browser via WASM, and all content is machine-readable structured data so third parties can build on it. The project targets absolute beginners — self-learners, public-library patrons, under-resourced school students, career-changers — and operates under a donated-compute lane with no server-side execution of learner code and no partner confirmed yet (verifiedNeed:false). The very first structural decision — authoring format — must be locked before any lesson is written or any schema/runner built, because it determines the shape of every downstream artifact. A wrong or deferred decision forces a painful migration later.
objective: Evaluate JSON-first vs Markdown-with-front-matter (compiled to JSON) as the canonical authoring format, weigh schema complexity, tooling ergonomics, and runner coupling, and record a binding decision with rationale before any seed authoring begins.
acceptanceCriteria: Both options (JSON-first and Markdown+front-matter compiled to JSON) are evaluated against criteria: schema validation complexity, author ergonomics, runner coupling, build determinism, and accessibility tooling fit.
A binding decision is recorded in a decision document committed to the repository, with explicit rationale for the chosen format and the trade-offs accepted.
The decision is made before any seed lesson authoring (occ-lesson-005) or schema authoring (occ-schema-002) begins.
Schema, validation tooling, and runner contracts are confirmed to target the chosen format.
Document is technically reviewed by the Maintainer.
output: A committed decision document in the repository recording the chosen authoring format, evaluation criteria, rationale, and implications for schema, tooling, and runner design.
